findings.text: Accept pending processor start-up signals for a virtual CPU. When no initialization or start-up signal is latched the operation is a no-op success. In nested guest operation it first consults nested event handling, treating a busy indication as deferred success while propagating other failures, and continues with local handling even after a nested exit. If platform state disallows the signals the start-up latch is discarded. Otherwise a latched initialization triggers a full CPU reset plus a multiprocessor state update, and a latched start-up signal is delivered only from the initialized-received state before marking the CPU runnable.

Multiprocessor start-up sequencing distinguishes bootstrap and application processors. Initialization moves a bootstrap processor directly to runnable and an application processor to initialized-received. A start-up signal has effect only while in initialized-received, delivering its vector and moving to runnable. Otherwise it is consumed without effect. Disallowed state clears the start-up latch without transition.

Nested event poll gives priority to a pending triple fault request over the vendor nested check. A triple fault invokes the nested triple-fault handler and reports an event pending. Otherwise the result of the vendor nested check is returned.

Virtual CPU reset establishes baseline architectural state for both power-on reset and initialization events. It exits nested guest context when active, resets local APIC state, clears execution flags and pending exception, interrupt, non-maskable and management-mode activity, reinitializes debug, control, segment-related and model-specific state, and applies vendor reset hooks plus control-register and exception-bitmap updates.

Reset clears queued and injected exception and interrupt indications, system-management pending counts, queued and pending non-maskable indications, debug breakpoint storage with effective-register refresh to architected defaults, second control register, event-request indication, asynchronous page-fault and steal-time model state, guest clock, and asynchronous fault queues, and marks the guest halted-for-fault flag false.

General registers are zeroed except the data register which reflects processor identification leaf one when present else a legacy family-model-stepping fallback. Instruction pointer and flags are set to architected reset values, stack pointer cache is marked dirty, third control register is zeroed and marked dirty, and control registers zero and four plus extended feature enable are installed through vendor setters followed by an exception-bitmap refresh. Cache-disable and not-write-through bits in control register zero are preserved on initialization and forced on reset.

Translation flushing on reset depends on prior paging and event type. Previously enabled paging requests a guest translation flush and a memory-management context reset. Initialization always requests an additional guest translation flush regardless of vendor, treating the flush as benign even where hardware might preserve entries.

Model-specific register writes pass through a common validator before reaching the vendor setter. Segment bases, kernel segment base and system-call targets require canonical addresses. System-enter pointers are canonicalized to host width. Time-stamp auxiliary requires platform support plus feature enablement and enforces vendor-specific reserved-bit handling with truncation to low half. Control-flow enforcement registers require shadow-stack or branch-tracking enablement with value legality checks. Shadow-stack pointers require shadow-stack support, sixty-four-bit support for the interrupt table variant, canonical alignment-constrained addresses, and host-only origin for the internal guest pointer.

User and supervisor control-flow enforcement values are legal only with reserved bits clear, with shadow-stack gated bits clear absent shadow-stack support and branch-tracking gated bits clear absent branch-tracking support, with the legacy bitmap base four-byte aligned, and without simultaneous suppress and wait-for-endbranch indications.

Extended control register updates accept only the feature-enabled mask index, require the floating-point bit, enforce that vector extension implies streaming extension, restrict to host-supported bits plus floating point, require paired bound-register bits, require all-or-nothing vector grouping with vector dependency, require all-or-nothing tile grouping, store the new mask, and mark dynamic identification bits dirty when extended-state bits change.

Extended processor state handling on reset is a no-op for power-on reset or absent floating state. On initialization it intersects host-supported save and supervisor masks with bound and control-flow components, unloads guest floating state when loaded, clears each selected component in memory, then reloads when previously loaded.

Flag updates through the common setter always request an event check after installing flags. The low-level installer preserves single-step debugging by forcing the trap bit when single-step is armed and the current linear instruction pointer matches the recorded single-step address, then delegates to the vendor flag setter.

Breakpoint register effective values track ownership. Without host breakpoint use, data breakpoint effective values follow guest values and debug control follows the guest control value. With host use they follow host debug values. Installing debug control goes through the vendor setter and refreshes a switch-needed flag that is set exactly when any breakpoint-enable bit is present.

Register caching uses paired availability and dirty bits per register with three legal combinations. Unavailable and clean means the value lives in hardware structures. Available and clean means cached in the virtual CPU structure. Available and dirty means cached and needing writeback. Unavailable plus dirty is invalid. Marking dirty sets both bits, instruction pointer writes store then mark dirty, control register zero and four reads cover all bits, and control register three is fetched into the cache on first use.

Register cache access is permitted only in task context or during performance-monitor handling in guest context. Use from general interrupt context can race cache updates, clobbering state or observing stale values, because availability and dirty marking are not atomic.

Bootstrap identity derives from the bootstrap flag in the local APIC base register. Setting multiprocessor state to runnable also clears the paravirtual unhalted indication. Other states leave it unchanged.

Local APIC enablement requires both hardware presence and software enablement. Latched initialization is reported only for kernel-emulated APICs with the initialization pending bit set. Raising an interrupt request sets the vector in the request bitmap before marking the aggregate pending flag, preserving the clear-side race order.

Start-up vector sampling must observe the pending latch before the vector byte, enforced by a read barrier between latch evaluation and vector load. Similarly the interrupt pending flag must be stored after the bitmap update so concurrent clearing cannot miss a pending vector.

Virtual local APIC state holds a base address, a memory-mapped I/O device, an embedded timer, a divide count, a back pointer to the virtual CPU, activity and enable flags including virtual-interrupt and guest-protection modes, a received-interrupt pending flag, a local-vector mode flag, an in-service count plus a highest-vector cache, a guest-visible register page with one-to-one layout, a virtual APIC address with translation cache, a pending-event bitmap, a start-up vector byte, and a local-vector-table length.

Local APIC timer state combines a high-resolution timer, a nanosecond period, a target expiration, mode and mode-mask words, a deadline and an expired-deadline value, a timer-advance adjustment, an atomic count of accumulated expirations, and a flag for hypervisor timer use.

Destination mapping state carries a reclamation header, a logical-mode selector, a maximum identifier, a union providing either a flat table of eight entries or a cluster table of sixteen by four entries, and a trailing flexible physical table.

Local APIC mode selector distinguishes disabled, invalid, legacy and extended states derived from enable bits. Logical destination mode distinguishes software-disabled, clustered legacy, flat legacy, extended, and mapping-disabled configurations. Local-vector-table positions enumerate timer, thermal, performance, two local interrupts, error and machine-check sources followed by a count sentinel.

Destination map lifetime is set up for deferred reclamation through its header, implying readers rely on read-side protection while updates replace and free asynchronously. Timer expirations accumulate in an atomic counter, allowing concurrent timer and virtual CPU paths to record firings without additional locking shown here.

Initialization latch occupies bit position zero and start-up latch occupies bit position one. Short-hand selector mask equals 786432, no-short-hand selector equals 0, destination mask bit equals 2048. Default bus cycle is one nanosecond. Legacy broadcast identifier equals 255 and extended broadcast identifier equals 4294967295. Extended register to model number translation shifts the register offset right by four places then adds the APIC base model number.

Legacy bitmap base for control-flow enforcement is the register value shifted right by twelve places. Table-walk memory-management enablement is fixed false in this header. Both local APIC and memory-management headers define private include guards.
Local APIC teardown flushes deferred disable branches for hardware and software paths and warns if either branch remains taken, indicating lingering users at module exit.
